Çatalhöyük. A Neolithic settlement in central Turkey that was occupied from around 7500 to 5700 BCE, representing one of the world's oldest cities and earliest examples of urban living. Located on the Konya Plain in central Anatolia, it was one of the largest Neolithic settlements ever discovered, covering 32 acres at its peak. The settlement was occupied continuously for nearly two thousand years, providing an unparalleled archaeological record through multiple layers of habitation.

What made Çatalhöyük so unusual was its radical approach to housing. The houses were mud-brick structures built directly adjacent to one another with no street access—inhabitants had to enter through roof hatches and used roofways to move between buildings. This honeycomb arrangement reveals experiments in communal living that predate the civilizations of Mesopotamia. The walls were decorated with elaborate murals featuring hunting scenes, geometric patterns, and hand prints—some of the oldest known monumental art.

The population at its peak is estimated at between five thousand and ten thousand inhabitants, rivaling or exceeding the size of contemporary settlements in Mesopotamia. The dead were buried beneath house floors, sometimes within months of death, suggesting strong ties between the living and ancestor veneration. Excavations by archaeologist James Mellaart between 1961 and 1965, and renewed work under Ian Hodder, revealed sophisticated gender roles, communal grain storage, and early religious practices.
